3:Referring to FIG. 1, the drilling jig includes an elongated straight rail 10. The rail 10 has a flat lower face 14 (FIG. 4) that rests on the front face of a workpiece 90, and an opposite upper face 12 (FIG. 3). A straight longitudinal slot 16 (FIG. 2) runs through the rail 10 from the upper face 12 to the lower face 14 and extends along the length of the rail 10. Distance marks 18 (FIG. 2) are carried on the upper face 12 beside the longitudinal slot 16 and are printed there. The rail 10 has a first end and an opposite second end.
17:The construction of the guide carriages is shown in FIG. 3, a cross-sectional view taken on line 3-3 of FIG. 2 through the second guide carriage 70, and in FIG. 5, a cross-sectional view taken on line 5-5 of FIG. 2 through the first guide carriage 50. The two guide carriages are of the same construction. Each guide carriage has a body that seats on the upper face 12 of the rail 10 and a key that depends from the body and passes into the longitudinal slot 16. The first guide carriage 50 has a key 52 (FIG. 5) and the second guide carriage 70 has a like key 72 (FIG. 3). The key 52 prevents rotation of the first guide carriage 50 relative to the rail 10 while permitting the first guide carriage 50 to slide along the longitudinal slot 16, and the key 72 does the same for the second guide carriage 70.
19:Each guide carriage carries one cylindrical drill bushing, a drill bushing 54 (FIG. 5) in the first guide carriage 50 and a drill bushing 74 (FIG. 3) in the second guide carriage 70. Each drill bushing has a bore that passes completely through the guide carriage that carries it and registers with the longitudinal slot 16, so that a drill bit passed down that bore travels through the longitudinal slot 16 and reaches the front face of the workpiece 90 beneath the rail 10. The bore of the drill bushing 54 of the first guide carriage 50 and the bore of the drill bushing 74 of the second guide carriage 70 are parallel to one another and perpendicular to the flat lower face 14 of the rail 10, and the key 52 and the key 72 hold their guide carriages against rotation relative to the rail 10 during the drilling, so that each hole is started and driven square to the front face of the workpiece 90 at the position set on the rail 10.
23:Each guide carriage has a threaded clamp knob above the rail 10, a clamp knob 58 (FIG. 5) on the first guide carriage 50 and a clamp knob 78 (FIG. 3) on the second guide carriage 70. A threaded shank of the clamp knob passes downward through the body of the guide carriage and through the longitudinal slot 16 and is received in a clamping shoe below the rail 10, a clamping shoe 60 (FIG. 5) in the case of the first guide carriage 50 and a clamping shoe 80 (FIG. 3) in the case of the second guide carriage 70. Turning the clamp knob in the tightening direction draws the clamping shoe upward toward the guide carriage, so that the rail 10 is clamped between the body of the guide carriage bearing on the upper face 12 and the clamping shoe bearing on the lower face 14. The guide carriage is thereby locked at a chosen position along the rail 10. Turning the clamp knob in the loosening direction releases the clamping shoe from the lower face 14 and permits the guide carriage to slide freely along the longitudinal slot 16. The clamping shoe 60 and the clamping shoe 80 are each disposed below the lower face 14 of the rail 10 and bear against the lower face 14 when the clamp knob 58 and the clamp knob 78 respectively are tightened, and each is released from the lower face 14 when the clamp knob of its guide carriage is loosened.
29:Referring to FIG. 7, the rail 10 has a transverse center index 24 at its midpoint. The transverse center index 24 is a mark that runs across the rail 10 transverse to the length of the rail 10 and marks the point midway between the ends of the rail 10. A shallow V-shaped sight notch 26 (FIG. 7) is formed in the second end of the rail 10 and is aligned with the transverse center index 24, for alignment with a pencil centerline 94 (FIG. 7) drawn on the workpiece 90. The transverse center index 24 and the sight notch 26 are aligned with one another, and the user aligns the transverse center index 24 and the sight notch 26 with the centerline 94 before drilling.
31:The settings of the jig are made as follows. The fence 30, with or without the spacer plate 40, sets the setback of both holes from the workpiece edge 92. The readings of the first pointer 62 and the second pointer 82 against the distance marks 18 set the separation between the two holes and the position of the pair relative to the centerline 94. The transverse center index 24 and the sight notch 26 are aligned with the centerline 94.
33:A method of locating and guiding the pair of holes with the jig is carried out as follows. The user first selects the center-to-center spacing of the pull to be installed. The clamp knob 58 and the clamp knob 78 are loosened. The first guide carriage 50 and the second guide carriage 70 are slid along the longitudinal slot 16 until the reading of the first pointer 62 and the reading of the second pointer 82 against the distance marks 18 differ by the selected spacing and are centered about the transverse center index 24, that is, until the two readings lie at equal distances on opposite sides of the transverse center index 24. The clamp knob 58 and the clamp knob 78 are then tightened, locking each guide carriage to the rail 10.
35:The user marks a centerline 94 on the front face of the workpiece 90 and places the flat lower face 14 of the rail 10 on that front face. Where an increased setback is wanted, the spacer plate 40 is fitted between the downwardly projecting portion 32 and the workpiece edge 92 before the downwardly projecting portion 32 is pressed against that edge. The downwardly projecting portion 32 of the fence 30, or the outer face of the spacer plate 40 when the spacer plate 40 is fitted, is pressed against the selected workpiece edge 92, which fixes the setback. The jig is then slid along the workpiece edge 92 until the sight notch 26 and the transverse center index 24 are aligned with the centerline 94. Holding the jig in that position, the user drills through the drill bushing 54 of the first guide carriage 50 and through the drill bushing 74 of the second guide carriage 70. The jig is then lifted away from the workpiece 90. No part of the jig remains attached to the workpiece 90, and the workpiece 90 carries only the two guided holes and the pencil centerline 94.
41:The jig is a hand tool and is operated entirely by hand. It is held against the front face of the workpiece 90 by hand during the drilling, and no part of it remains attached to the workpiece 90. The jig has no motor, no battery, no electronic sensor, and no network connection. Every setting is made mechanically and is read directly from the distance marks 18, the transverse center index 24, and the sight notch 26.

The invention is a reusable hand tool that locates and guides two drill holes for a cabinet pull without requiring a powered measuring system. Distance marks are printed along the upper face beside the slot.

A fixed fence is attached at the first end of the rail. The fence extends downward from the lower face and bears against one straight edge of the workpiece. The fence is perpendicular to the rail, so the rail extends inward across the workpiece when the fence bears against the edge. A removable spacer plate can be fitted between the fence and the workpiece edge. The spacer plate has parallel opposite faces and changes the setback of every guided hole by its thickness without changing the separation between the holes.

Two separate guide carriages sit on the upper face of the rail. Each carriage has a lower key that passes into the longitudinal slot, and the key prevents the carriage from rotating while allowing it to slide along the slot. Each carriage carries one cylindrical drill bushing with a vertical bore. The bore passes completely through the carriage and aligns with an opening through the slot so a drill bit can reach the workpiece. The two bushing axes are parallel to one another and perpendicular to the flat lower face of the rail.

Each carriage has a threaded clamp knob above the rail. A threaded shank of the knob passes through the carriage and the longitudinal slot into a clamping shoe below the rail. Turning the knob draws the shoe toward the carriage and clamps the rail between the carriage and the shoe. Loosening the knob allows the carriage to slide. The first carriage has a pointer aligned with its bushing axis and readable against the distance marks. The second carriage has its own pointer aligned with its bushing axis. The difference between the two pointer readings is therefore the center-to-center hole spacing.

The rail has a transverse center index at its midpoint. A shallow V-shaped sight notch is formed in the second end of the rail and aligned with the center index. The user can align the center index and the sight notch with a pencil centerline on the workpiece before tightening both carriage knobs. The fence controls setback from the workpiece edge, while the two pointer readings control hole separation and the position of the pair relative to the centerline.

The fence is reversible. It is secured to the first end of the rail by two screws received in two corresponding holes. Removing the screws, turning the fence over, and reinstalling the screws moves the downwardly projecting part of the fence from one longitudinal side of the rail to the opposite longitudinal side. This lets the same marked upper face be used when the tool is referenced from either an upper edge or a lower edge of a workpiece.

To use the tool, the user selects the desired hole spacing, loosens both clamp knobs, slides the carriages until their pointer readings have the desired difference and are centered about the transverse center index, and tightens the knobs. The user places the lower face on the workpiece, presses the fence or the installed spacer plate against the selected workpiece edge, aligns the sight notch and center index with the pencil centerline, and drills through both bushings. The tool is then lifted away. No part remains attached to the workpiece.

**FIG. 4** — the renderer's "unexpected" small rectangle on the rail's upper side is in fact the disclosed longitudinal slot seen end-on (the disclosure states the slot runs through the rail from upper face to lower face). Rather than banning the linework, I made the geometry expected by describing it: the slot is now stated to appear in this end-on view as a narrow opening in the rail's upper side, and numeral 16 is added to the sheet's list (8 numerals, at the cap).

**FIG. 7** — the leader for 24 landed on a crosshair because the transverse index mark was drawn spanning the band and therefore crossing the longitudinal slot, while the workpiece centerline was described as aligned through the same point. Both crossings are removed: the index is now one straight stroke of visible thickness lying in the strip of upper surface between one long side of the band and the neighbouring side of the slot, clear of the slot, and the centerline is drawn on the workpiece alone as two collinear segments starting at the long sides of the band and running outward. That gives numeral 24 a single isolated body to terminate on.

FIG. 7: the leader for numeral 24 terminated on a crosshair because the transverse center index was described as spanning the band and therefore crossing the longitudinal slot, while the workpiece centerline was described as aligned through the same crossing point. The index is now a single straight stroke of visible thickness occupying the strip of upper surface between one long side of the band and the neighbouring side of the slot, standing clear of the slot, and the centerline is drawn on the workpiece alone as two collinear segments running outward from the long sides of the band. reasoning: The FIG. 4 failure was a mismatch between brief and render, not an invention question. The rail is drawn end-on and the disclosure states a straight longitudinal slot runs through the rail from upper face to lower face, so an opening in the upper side is the truthful reading of the rendered rectangle. Legitimising it in the brief is source-faithful and avoids writing a generic negative ban on linework, which the drafting rules forbid.

In FIG. 4 I wrote 'upper side' rather than the canonical part name 'upper face 12', because numeral 12 is not carried on that sheet and naming the part canonically without its numeral on a sheet that does not list it is the sort of stale reference the numeral check flags.

The root cause of the FIG. 7 leader defect was geometric, not typographic: a transverse mark spanning the band necessarily crosses the lengthwise slot, and the centerline was additionally described as aligned with both the index and the sight notch, so the only place a dot could land for numeral 24 was an intersection of three lines. Separating the index from the slot and keeping the centerline off the rail gives the terminator one isolated body of visible thickness to sit on.

A single ragged break at the left means the omitted portion runs toward the first end, so the index sitting just inside the break is the midpoint, which is consistent; and a full-length plan of the rail would have had to show the first end without the fence that the disclosure fixes there.

3	A perspective view of a drilling jig on a workpiece 90.
4	
5	The workpiece 90 is a flat panel, and one straight side of the panel is the workpiece edge 92.
6

The fence 30 has a downwardly projecting portion 32 that stands on the longitudinal side of the rail 10 that faces the workpiece edge 92, extends below the rail 10, and contacts the workpiece edge 92.
8	
9	Two guide carriages, a first guide carriage 50 and a second guide carriage 70, rest on top of the rail 10, the first guide carriage 50 nearer the fence 30 and the second guide carriage 70 farther from the fence 30. Each guide carriage is shown schematically as a plain block. A clamp knob 58 stands above the first guide carriage 50 and a clamp knob 78 stands above the second guide carriage 70, each shown schematically as a plain round body.
10

1	In the following description, the terms upper, lower, above, below, inward, and downward refer to the orientation of the drilling jig when its flat lower face rests on the front face of a workpiece. These terms are used for convenience of description and do not limit the orientation in which the jig may be used.
2	
3	Referring to FIG. 1, the drilling jig includes an elongated straight rail 10. The rail 10 has a flat lower face 14 (FIG. 4) that rests on the front face of a workpiece 90, and an opposite upper face 12 (FIG. 3). A straight longitudinal slot 16 (FIG. 2) runs through the rail 10 from the upper face 12 to the lower face 14 and extends along the length of the rail 10. Distance marks 18 (FIG. 2) are carried on the upper face 12 beside the longitudinal slot 16 and are printed there. The rail 10 has a first end and an opposite second end.
4	
5	The workpiece 90 is a cabinet door or a drawer front having a front face and at least one straight workpiece edge 92. The jig locates and guides the two holes for a cabinet pull, and it does so in a single placement of the jig on the front face of the workpiece 90.
6	
7	A fence 30 is secured to the first end of the rail 10. The fence 30 is a fixed fence, by which is meant that it occupies a fixed position at the first end of the rail 10 and is not slidable along the rail 10 as the guide carriages described below are. No setting of the jig is made by moving the fence 30 along the rail 10, and no position along the length of the rail 10 other than the first end is available to it. A fixed fence in this sense is not a permanent one. As described below, the fence 30 is releasably secured to the rail 10 and may be taken off and reinstalled in either of two orientations, and it occupies the same fixed position at the first end of the rail 10 in both of those orientations. The fence 30 includes a downwardly projecting portion 32 that stands on one longitudinal side of the rail 10 and extends below the lower face 14 of the rail 10. As seen in FIG. 1, the downwardly projecting portion 32 bears against the workpiece edge 92. The fence 30 is perpendicular to the rail 10, so that when the downwardly projecting portion 32 is held against the workpiece edge 92 the rail 10 extends inward across the front face of the workpiece 90. The fence 30 therefore fixes the setback of the jig, and of every hole guided by the jig, from the workpiece edge 92.
8	
9	Referring to FIG. 6, the fence 30 is releasably secured to the first end of the rail 10 by two screws 34 received in two corresponding mounting holes 36. The fence 30 is reversible. In a first orientation, the downwardly projecting portion 32 lies on a first longitudinal side of the rail 10. The fence 30 is securable in a second orientation upon removal of the two screws 34, inversion of the fence 30, and reinstallation of the two screws 34 in the same two mounting holes 36, and in that second orientation the downwardly projecting portion 32 lies on the opposite second longitudinal side of the rail 10. In both orientations the upper face 12, and the distance marks 18 carried on it, face away from the workpiece 90 and remain visible to the user, and the distance marks 18 read in the same direction along the rail 10.
10	
11	The reversible mounting of the fence 30 addresses a practical difficulty of edge-referenced hole location. A pull on one cabinet component is commonly located from an upper edge of the component, while a pull on another component of the same run is commonly located from a lower edge. If the projecting part of an edge fence is permanently fixed to one longitudinal side of a marked rail, referencing the opposite edge requires either turning the whole tool over, which places the marked face against the panel where it cannot be read, or providing a second set of marks that runs in the opposite direction, which the user may read in error. Reversing the fence 30 alone moves the reference face to the other longitudinal side of the rail 10 while leaving the rail 10, the distance marks 18, and the carriage settings undisturbed.
12	
13	A removable spacer plate 40, shown in FIG. 4, may be fitted between the fence 30 and the workpiece edge 92. The spacer plate 40 has parallel opposite faces, one of which bears against the downwardly projecting portion 32 and the other of which bears against the workpiece edge 92. Because the two faces of the spacer plate 40 are parallel, the spacer plate 40 increases the setback of every hole guided by the jig by the thickness of the spacer plate 40 and does not change the separation between the holes. A second setback may therefore be obtained by fitting the spacer plate 40 without disturbing a hole spacing that has already been set. The spacer plate 40 is fitted between the fence 30 and the workpiece edge 92 and is removable.
14	
15	Referring again to FIG. 1, a first guide carriage 50 and a second guide carriage 70 are seated separately on the rail 10, one nearer to the fence 30 than the other. The two guide carriages are separate bodies that are uncoupled from one another, and each is positioned along the rail 10 and clamped to the rail 10 independently of the other.
16	
17	The construction of the guide carriages is shown in FIG. 3, a cross-sectional view taken on line 3-3 of FIG. 2 through the second guide carriage 70, and in FIG. 5, a cross-sectional view taken on line 5-5 of FIG. 2 through the first guide carriage 50. The two guide carriages are of the same construction. Each guide carriage has a body that seats on the upper face 12 of the rail 10 and a key that depends from the body and passes into the longitudinal slot 16. The first guide carriage 50 has a key 52 (FIG. 5) and the second guide carriage 70 has a like key 72 (FIG. 3). The key 52 prevents rotation of the first guide carriage 50 relative to the rail 10 while permitting the first guide carriage 50 to slide along the longitudinal slot 16, and the key 72 does the same for the second guide carriage 70.
18	
19	Each guide carriage carries one cylindrical drill bushing, a drill bushing 54 (FIG. 5) in the first guide carriage 50 and a drill bushing 74 (FIG. 3) in the second guide carriage 70. Each drill bushing has a bore that passes completely through the guide carriage that carries it and registers with the longitudinal slot 16, so that a drill bit passed down that bore travels through the longitudinal slot 16 and reaches the front face of the workpiece 90 beneath the rail 10. The bore of the drill bushing 54 of the first guide carriage 50 and the bore of the drill bushing 74 of the second guide carriage 70 are parallel to one another and perpendicular to the flat lower face 14 of the rail 10, and the key 52 and the key 72 hold their guide carriages against rotation relative to the rail 10 during the drilling, so that each hole is started and driven square to the front face of the workpiece 90 at the position set on the rail 10.
20	
21	The drill bushing 54 and the drill bushing 74 are wear parts. Each is made of hardened metal and is received in the body of its guide carriage as a separate piece that is withdrawable from that guide carriage, so that a worn drill bushing can be withdrawn from the guide carriage and replaced by another drill bushing.
22	
23	Each guide carriage has a threaded clamp knob above the rail 10, a clamp knob 58 (FIGS. 1 and 5) on the first guide carriage 50 and a clamp knob 78 (FIGS. 1 and 3) on the second guide carriage 70. A threaded shank of the clamp knob passes downward through the body of the guide carriage and through the longitudinal slot 16 and is received in a clamping shoe below the rail 10, a clamping shoe 60 (FIG. 5) in the case of the first guide carriage 50 and a clamping shoe 80 (FIG. 3) in the case of the second guide carriage 70. Turning the clamp knob in the tightening direction draws the clamping shoe upward toward the guide carriage, so that the rail 10 is clamped between the body of the guide carriage bearing on the upper face 12 and the clamping shoe bearing on the lower face 14. The guide carriage is thereby locked at a chosen position along the rail 10. Turning the clamp knob in the loosening direction releases the clamping shoe from the lower face 14 and permits the guide carriage to slide freely along the longitudinal slot 16. The clamping shoe 60 and the clamping shoe 80 are each disposed below the lower face 14 of the rail 10 and bear against the lower face 14 when the clamp knob 58 and the clamp knob 78 respectively are tightened, and each is released from the lower face 14 when the clamp knob of its guide carriage is loosened.
24	
25	The first guide carriage 50 carries a first pointer 62 and the second guide carriage 70 carries a second pointer 82, as seen in FIG. 2. The first pointer 62 is aligned with the axis of the bore of the drill bushing 54 of the first guide carriage 50 and is readable against the distance marks 18. The second pointer 82 is aligned with the axis of the bore of the drill bushing 74 of the second guide carriage 70 and is readable against the distance marks 18. Each pointer is an index feature that stands adjacent the distance marks 18 on the upper face 12.
26	
27	Because each guide carriage carries its own pointer and each pointer is read against the same distance marks 18, the position of each hole of the pair is established by its own direct reading. The difference between the reading of the first pointer 62 and the reading of the second pointer 82 is the center-to-center spacing of the two holes that the jig will guide. The position of each guide carriage along the rail 10 is therefore set by its own reading against the distance marks 18, independently of the position of the other guide carriage.
28	
29	Referring to FIG. 7, the rail 10 has a transverse center index 24 at its midpoint. The transverse center index 24 is a mark that runs across the rail 10 transverse to the length of the rail 10 and marks the point midway between the ends of the rail 10. A shallow V-shaped sight notch 26 (FIG. 7) is formed in the second end of the rail 10 and is aligned with the transverse center index 24, for alignment with a pencil centerline 94 (FIG. 7) drawn on the workpiece 90. The transverse center index 24 and the sight notch 26 are aligned with one another, and the user aligns the transverse center index 24 and the sight notch 26 with the centerline 94 before drilling.
30	
31	The settings of the jig are made as follows. The fence 30, with or without the spacer plate 40, sets the setback of both holes from the workpiece edge 92. The readings of the first pointer 62 and the second pointer 82 against the distance marks 18 set the separation between the two holes and the position of the pair relative to the centerline 94. The transverse center index 24 and the sight notch 26 are aligned with the centerline 94.
32	
33	A method of locating and guiding the pair of holes with the jig is carried out as follows. The user first selects the center-to-center spacing of the pull to be installed. The clamp knob 58 and the clamp knob 78 are loosened. The first guide carriage 50 and the second guide carriage 70 are slid along the longitudinal slot 16 until the reading of the first pointer 62 and the reading of the second pointer 82 against the distance marks 18 differ by the selected spacing and are centered about the transverse center index 24, that is, until the two readings lie at equal distances on opposite sides of the transverse center index 24. The clamp knob 58 and the clamp knob 78 are then tightened, locking each guide carriage to the rail 10.
34	
35	The user marks a centerline 94 on the front face of the workpiece 90 and places the flat lower face 14 of the rail 10 on that front face. Where an increased setback is wanted, the spacer plate 40 is fitted between the downwardly projecting portion 32 and the workpiece edge 92 before the downwardly projecting portion 32 is pressed against that edge. The downwardly projecting portion 32 of the fence 30, or the outer face of the spacer plate 40 when the spacer plate 40 is fitted, is pressed against the selected workpiece edge 92, which fixes the setback. Referring to FIG. 1, the drilling jig includes an elongated straight rail 10. The rail 10 has a flat lower face 14 (FIG. 4) that rests on the front face of a workpiece 90, and an opposite upper face 12 (FIG. 3). A straight longitudinal slot 16 (FIG. 2) runs through the rail 10 from the upper face 12 to the lower face 14 and extends along the length of the rail 10. Distance marks 18 (FIG. 2) are carried on the upper face 12 beside the longitudinal slot 16 and are printed there. The rail 10 has a first end and an opposite second end.

The workpiece 90 is a cabinet door or a drawer front having a front face and at least one straight workpiece edge 92. The jig locates and guides the two holes for a cabinet pull, and it does so in a single placement of the jig on the front face of the workpiece 90.

A fence 30 is secured to the first end of the rail 10. The fence 30 is a fixed fence, by which is meant that it occupies a fixed position at the first end of the rail 10 and is not slidable along the rail 10 as the guide carriages described below are. No setting of the jig is made by moving the fence 30 along the rail 10, and no position along the length of the rail 10 other than the first end is available to it. A fixed fence in this sense is not a permanent one. As described below, the fence 30 is releasably secured to the rail 10 and may be taken off and reinstalled in either of two orientations, and it occupies the same fixed position at the first end of the rail 10 in both of those orientations. The fence 30 includes a downwardly projecting portion 32 that stands on one longitudinal side of the rail 10 and extends below the lower face 14 of the rail 10. As seen in FIG. 1, the downwardly projecting portion 32 bears against the workpiece edge 92. The fence 30 is perpendicular to the rail 10, so that when the downwardly projecting portion 32 is held against the workpiece edge 92 the rail 10 extends inward across the front face of the workpiece 90. The fence 30 therefore fixes the setback of the jig, and of every hole guided by the jig, from the workpiece edge 92.

Referring to FIG. 6, the fence 30 is releasably secured to the first end of the rail 10 by two screws 34 received in two corresponding mounting holes 36. The fence 30 is reversible. In a first orientation, the downwardly projecting portion 32 lies on a first longitudinal side of the rail 10. The fence 30 is securable in a second orientation upon removal of the two screws 34, inversion of the fence 30, and reinstallation of the two screws 34 in the same two mounting holes 36, and in that second orientation the downwardly projecting portion 32 lies on the opposite second longitudinal side of the rail 10. In both orientations the upper face 12, and the distance marks 18 carried on it, face away from the workpiece 90 and remain visible to the user, and the distance marks 18 read in the same direction along the rail 10.

The reversible mounting of the fence 30 addresses a practical difficulty of edge-referenced hole location. A pull on one cabinet component is commonly located from an upper edge of the component, while a pull on another component of the same run is commonly located from a lower edge. If the projecting part of an edge fence is permanently fixed to one longitudinal side of a marked rail, referencing the opposite edge requires either turning the whole tool over, which places the marked face against the panel where it cannot be read, or providing a second set of marks that runs in the opposite direction, which the user may read in error. Reversing the fence 30 alone moves the reference face to the other longitudinal side of the rail 10 while leaving the rail 10, the distance marks 18, and the carriage settings undisturbed.

Because the two faces of the spacer plate 40 are parallel, the spacer plate 40 increases the setback of every hole guided by the jig by the thickness of the spacer plate 40 and does not change the separation between the holes. A second setback may therefore be obtained by fitting the spacer plate 40 without disturbing a hole spacing that has already been set. The spacer plate 40 is fitted between the fence 30 and the workpiece edge 92 and is removable.

Referring again to FIG. 1, a first guide carriage 50 and a second guide carriage 70 are seated separately on the rail 10, one nearer to the fence 30 than the other. The two guide carriages are separate bodies that are uncoupled from one another, and each is positioned along the rail 10 and clamped to the rail 10 independently of the other.

The two guide carriages are of the same construction. Each guide carriage has a body that seats on the upper face 12 of the rail 10 and a key that depends from the body and passes into the longitudinal slot 16. Each drill bushing has a bore that passes completely through the guide carriage that carries it and registers with the longitudinal slot 16, so that a drill bit passed down that bore travels through the longitudinal slot 16 and reaches the front face of the workpiece 90 beneath the rail 10. The clamp knob 58 and the clamp knob 78 are loosened. Every setting is made mechanically and is read directly from the distance marks 18, the transverse center index 24, and the sight notch 26.

Turning the clamp knob in the tightening direction draws the clamping shoe upward toward the guide carriage, so that the rail 10 is clamped between the body of the guide carriage bearing on the upper face 12 and the clamping shoe bearing on the lower face 14. The guide carriage is thereby locked at a chosen position along the rail 10. Turning the clamp knob in the loosening direction releases the clamping shoe from the lower face 14 and permits the guide carriage to slide freely along the longitudinal slot 16. The clamping shoe 60 and the clamping shoe 80 are each disposed below the lower face 14 of the rail 10 and bear against the lower face 14 when the clamp knob 58 and the clamp knob 78 respectively are tightened, and each is released from the lower face 14 when the clamp knob of its guide carriage is loosened.

The first guide carriage 50 carries a first pointer 62 and the second guide carriage 70 carries a second pointer 82, as seen in FIG. 2. The first pointer 62 is aligned with the axis of the bore of the drill bushing 54 of the first guide carriage 50 and is readable against the distance marks 18. The second pointer 82 is aligned with the axis of the bore of the drill bushing 74 of the second guide carriage 70 and is readable against the distance marks 18. Each pointer is an index feature that stands adjacent the distance marks 18 on the upper face 12.

Because each guide carriage carries its own pointer and each pointer is read against the same distance marks 18, the position of each hole of the pair is established by its own direct reading. The difference between the reading of the first pointer 62 and the reading of the second pointer 82 is the center-to-center spacing of the two holes that the jig will guide. The position of each guide carriage along the rail 10 is therefore set by its own reading against the distance marks 18, independently of the position of the other guide carriage.

Referring to FIG. 7, the rail 10 has a transverse center index 24 at its midpoint. The transverse center index 24 is a mark that runs across the rail 10 transverse to the length of the rail 10 and marks the point midway between the ends of the rail 10. A shallow V-shaped sight notch 26 (FIG. 7) is formed in the second end of the rail 10 and is aligned with the transverse center index 24, for alignment with a pencil centerline 94 (FIG. 7) drawn on the workpiece 90. The transverse center index 24 and the sight notch 26 are aligned with one another, and the user aligns the transverse center index 24 and the sight notch 26 with the centerline 94 before drilling.

The settings of the jig are made as follows. The fence 30, with or without the spacer plate 40, sets the setback of both holes from the workpiece edge 92. The readings of the first pointer 62 and the second pointer 82 against the distance marks 18 set the separation between the two holes and the position of the pair relative to the centerline 94. The transverse center index 24 and the sight notch 26 are aligned with the centerline 94.

A method of locating and guiding the pair of holes with the jig is carried out as follows. The user first selects the center-to-center spacing of the pull to be installed. The clamp knob 58 and the clamp knob 78 are loosened. The first guide carriage 50 and the second guide carriage 70 are slid along the longitudinal slot 16 until the reading of the first pointer 62 and the reading of the second pointer 82 against the distance marks 18 differ by the selected spacing and are centered about the transverse center index 24, that is, until the two readings lie at equal distances on opposite sides of the transverse center index 24. The clamp knob 58 and the clamp knob 78 are then tightened, locking each guide carriage to the rail 10.

The user marks a centerline 94 on the front face of the workpiece 90 and places the flat lower face 14 of the rail 10 on that front face. Where an increased setback is wanted, the spacer plate 40 is fitted between the downwardly projecting portion 32 and the workpiece edge 92 before the downwardly projecting portion 32 is pressed against that edge. The downwardly projecting portion 32 of the fence 30, or the outer face of the spacer plate 40 when the spacer plate 40 is fitted, is pressed against the selected workpiece edge 92, which fixes the setback. The sight notch 26 and the transverse center index 24 are then aligned with the centerline 94. Holding the jig in that position, the user drills through the drill bushing 54 of the first guide carriage 50 and through the drill bushing 74 of the second guide carriage 70. The jig is then lifted away from the workpiece 90. No part of the jig remains attached to the workpiece 90, and the workpiece 90 carries only the two guided holes and the pencil centerline 94.

When the next component of the run is to be referenced from the opposite edge, after the jig has been lifted away from the workpiece 90, the user removes the two screws 34, turns the fence 30 over, and reinstalls the two screws 34 in the two mounting holes 36. The downwardly projecting portion 32 then stands on the opposite longitudinal side of the rail 10, the upper face 12 still faces the user, and the carriage settings and the reading direction of the distance marks 18 are unchanged. The jig is used on the second component in the same way as on the first.

The rail 10, the fence 30, the bodies of the first guide carriage 50 and the second guide carriage 70, the clamping shoe 60 and the clamping shoe 80, the spacer plate 40, the first pointer 62, the second pointer 82, and the clamp knob 58 and the clamp knob 78 may be made of rigid polymer or of metal. The drill bushing 54 and the drill bushing 74 are made of hardened metal.

The jig is a hand tool and is operated entirely by hand. It is held against the front face of the workpiece 90 by hand during the drilling, and no part of it remains attached to the workpiece 90. The jig has no motor, no battery, no electronic sensor, and no network connection. Every setting is made mechanically and is read directly from the distance marks 18, the transverse center index 24, and the sight notch 26.

The foregoing description of embodiments is illustrative. The features described above may be used in combinations other than those expressly described, and the scope of protection sought is defined by the claims that follow.

input.summary: Resolved the single QA blocker (FIG. 1 carried 9 reference numerals, over the 8-per-sheet limit) by moving the two clamp knobs off the overview sheet and onto the focused section sheets that already detail them, then resynchronizing the Detailed Description figure callouts. Also brought the FIG. 2 brief under the 2800-character cap and gave both cutting-plane lines explicit physical endpoints. No other file was touched; claims, numerals table, and background are unchanged.
reasoning: The blocker was purely a drawing-load problem, not a disclosure problem, so the fix had to shed numerals from FIG. 1 without shedding any disclosed structure. FIG. 3 and FIG. 5 are already focused sectional views taken through the second and first guide carriages, and each one shows its clamp knob together with the threaded shank passing through the carriage and the longitudinal slot into the clamping shoe below the rail. Those sheets are where the knob is actually explained, so numerals 58 and 78 belong there and nowhere else. Creating an eighth sheet to hold two numerals that two existing sheets already carry would have added a drawing that teaches nothing new.

Having removed the numerals from FIG. 1, I removed the canonical part name 'clamp knob' from that brief too, since a part name on a sheet whose numeral list does not include it is exactly the kind of desynchronization the review catches. The knobs still need to be visible in a perspective overview of the assembled jig, so they remain as an unnumbered plain round body above each carriage block, identified as shown schematically. That is a depiction convention only, and I added nothing about its shape or proportion to the specification or claims.

The Detailed Description previously told the examiner that clamp knob 58 was visible in FIGS. 1 and 5 and clamp knob 78 in FIGS. 1 and 3. Leaving that would have created a text-to-figure mismatch in the opposite direction, so both callouts now name only the sectional sheet that shows the part. I checked the other two FIG. 1 callouts in the description: the paragraph introducing the rail and the paragraph on the downwardly projecting portion bearing against the workpiece edge both refer only to parts still listed on FIG. 1, and parts named there that live on other sheets already carry their own parenthetical cross-references.

The FIG. 2 brief stood at 2947 characters, above the 2800 cap. The two cutting-plane paragraphs repeated each other almost verbatim, so I condensed the second to refer back to the construction of the first rather than restating it. I used the space recovered to state each line's physical endpoints, which the section-line rule requires and which the earlier wording only implied: each line begins clear of one long side of the rail and ends clear of the other.
